articles.title: Brazil to shorten workweek in win for Lula ahead of runoff
articles.summary: Brazil's Senate approved cutting the workweek from 44 to 40 hours. The move could give President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva an edge over his opponent, Flavio Bolsonaro, ahead of the October 25 runoff.

image.caption: Amendment lowers working hours from 44 hours a week to 40, providing Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva a key legislative win ahead of Oct. 25 runoff [Photo: October 11]Image: Paulo Lopes/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Brazil's Senate on Thursday approved a constitutional amendment to reduce the working week to five days from six without a salary cut, likely providing President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva with an edge ahead of Flavio Bolsonaro in the presidential runoff on October 25.
Lula is expected to sign the shorter workweek into law next week.

Brazil's leftist leader has taken a number of steps in recent days to shore up support before the runoff, including new fuel tax cuts, extending existing subsidies and pledging to pardon the debts of more than 3.6 million small businesses to the federal government and others.
But the pledge to trim the workweek turned into a top promise that Lula hoped to deliver on before the runoff.
Brazil election: Lula faces Flavio Bolsonaro in runoff
"6x1" reform receives overwhelming support
The new amendment, known as the "6x1" reform, could benefit more than 37 million workers, according to the government.
"The end of the 6x1 is more than a change in the workday. It's more time to live, rest, be with family, watch your children grow, take care of yourself, and enjoy life," Lula wrote on X.
"Those who work so hard to build Brazil also deserve time to live. It's a victory for workers. It's Brazil ready for more," he said.
But the legislation still leaves out a large number of people in the shadow economy, like freelancers and delivery drivers.
Lula, a former trade unionist, worked on the proposal to reduce the workweek with his government over the course of the year.
Bolsonaro backs "6x1" reform after opposing it

Flavio Bolsonaro, a right-wing senator and the eldest son of imprisoned former President Jair Bolsonaro, had long opposed the legislation. But Flavio Bolsonaro reversed course on Tuesday to say that he'll back the bill because it has so much support.

Many businesses opposed the bill because it would raise their costs, and Bolsonaro previously argued for estabilishing a flexible payment regime where individuals negotiate their pay with their employers.
He repeatedly called the legislation election-motivated.
In the first round of elections earlier this month, Bolsonaro dealt Lula a bruising defeat, finishing ahead with 47% of the vote, though short of the 50% needed for an outright majority.
The campaign in Brazil has been dominated by voter frustration over high street crime, the strength of Evangelical churches, the high tax burden for businesses and economic dissatisfaction.

articles.title: El Niño damage to agriculture hits P6.8 billion
articles.summary: Agricultural damage has reached P6.8 billion this year as several areas struggle with dry spells linked to the very strong El Niño phenomenon in recent months.

blocks.text: October 15, 2026 | 11:13am
Farm workers check on their crops, spray organic pesticides, and remove unwanted weeds at a rice field in Tanay, Rizal on Sept. 19, 2023.
Ernie Penaredondo

MANILA, Philippines — Agricultural damage has reached P6.8 billion this year as several areas struggle with dry spells linked to the very strong El Niño phenomenon in recent months, according to the Office of Civil Defense (OCD).

OCD spokesperson Junie Castillo said on Thursday, October 15, that while the amount accounts for the total damage recorded this year, the reduced water supply for irrigation due to lower rainfall has negatively affected crop production in some areas over the past two months.

“May mga nakaranas na nung dry spells at drought. Ibig sabihin, mga two months na bawas na sa mga pag-ulan, kaya ‘yung mga patubig sa mga agrikultura, kaya nagkaroon na rin ng kabawasan sa produksyon ng iba’t ibang crops sa iba’t ibang lugar,” Castillo said in an interview with dzMM.

(Some areas have already experienced dry spells and drought. That means rainfall has been reduced for the past two months, and so has irrigation for agriculture, resulting in a decline in the production of different crops across different areas.)

The agency added that, as of press time, 109 areas had already declared a state of calamity due to the impacts of El Niño, with most local government units expressing concerns over agricultural damage.
Concerns on rice, vegetable supplies

The Philippine Chamber of Agriculture and Food Inc., a private-sector group focused on agribusiness and food security, has also expressed concerns about the impacts of El Niño on the agriculture sector, including vegetable and rice supplies.

The group’s president, Danilo Fausto, said on Thursday, October 15, in a separate interview with dzRH that the rice supply of the National Food Authority (NFA) is currently insufficient and may last only 51 days, instead of the ideal 70 to 90 days.

He also warned that several factors, including the depreciation of the peso, rising importation costs, and the impact of El Niño on other countries from which the Philippines usually imports rice, may drive up domestic rice prices.

Fausto also said that while vegetable production is currently in favorable condition and is expected to remain so until the end of 2026, harvests may decline by the first quarter of next year as dry conditions worsen.

“We are expecting this last quarter meron tayong mga gulay…kasi maganda ang harvest natin. Ang problema pagdating mo next year ng first quarter towards March tuyot na ‘yan so hindi masyadong lalaki ang mga gulay,” Fausto said.

(We are expecting this last quarter that we will have vegetables… because our harvests are good. The problem is when drought comes in the first quarter towards March next year, the vegetables may no longer grow properly.)
Gov’t interventions

The OCD said the government has provided about P10 billion worth of assistance, particularly through the Department of Agriculture (DA), to help farmers prepare for the anticipated worsening dry conditions.
According to Castillo, the assistance included the distribution of water pumps, seeds and fertilizers, as well as livelihood support programs.

He also mentioned that the government has a National Action Plan for El Niño to monitor and address the situation in the areas of food security, water security, health security, energy and public safety during the phenomenon.

The state weather bureau PAGASA had earlier reported that drought may affect all provinces in the country in March 2027, warning the public of potential El Niño risks such as water shortages and heat-related illnesses.

articles.title: Texas Democrat James Talarico faces grilling from voters at town hall in tight Senate race
articles.summary:
Talarico casts himself as a moderate who would put Texans’ needs over party allegiances amid close contest against Republican Ken Paxton

James Talarico, the Texas Democratic nominee for…

blocks.text: James Talarico, the Texas Democratic nominee for Senate, sat face to face with several undecided voters who grilled him on a slew of contentious issues including Israel’s military campaign in Gaza, abortion and foreign aid, during a CNN town hall on Wednesday evening.
One voter, a devout small business owner, questioned the authenticity of Talarico’s faith, referencing a past remark where he described God as nonbinary.

“When I said that, I was being provocative and I want to admit that and come clean about that,” Talarico responded. “What I was saying is actually not controversial theologically: the idea that we can’t define God using human categories. Not only did I say that, but the late Charlie Kirk said that – the late Pope Benedict said that.”
Talarico added that he was receptive to feedback from Christians.

Jodi Hunt, a self-described single-issue voter, probed Talarico’s pro-choice stance, asking: “How would you convince me as a Catholic voter that I can trust you would protect the most innocent among us?”
Talarico described the Bible as being silent on abortion, to which Hunt countered quoting “Thou shalt not kill”.

“We may have different, moral conclusions when it comes to this particular ethical question, but we actually have the same public policy goal,” Talarico said, framing abortion as a public health issue that could be solved with a reduction in unplanned pregnancies.
During the night, Talarico cast himself as a moderate, who would put the needs of Texans over party allegiances. He railed against the ultra-wealthy, framing them as the common enemy.

Talarico and the Republican nominee, Ken Paxton, are locked in a competitive race to become Texas’s next US senator, with most recent polls showing Talarico with a narrow lead over Paxton. (Paxton declined an invitation to appear on CNN, host Erin Burnett said at the start of the town hall.)

Though Democrats have not won a Senate seat in the state since the late 1980s, they’re hoping Talarico’s newcomer energy and popular appeal will persuade independents and Republicans fed up with Donald Trump’s second term – or turned off by Paxton’s many scandals.

Over the weekend, Talarico became the subject of a disinformation campaign after he was absent from the campaign trail for more than a week. While Talarico’s campaign repeatedly said the candidate was sick with a bad case of the flu, conservative influencers falsely accused him of receiving medical treatment at a mental health facility in Ohio.
The rumor was further propelled by Paxton and Trump, who sought to fuel skepticism about Talarico’s health and fitness for office.
The Democratic candidate denied the false allegations after returning to the campaign trail last week, noting he had never been to Ohio.

“False claims got millions of views online and this is an example of what I call the ‘rage economy’,” Talarico said during the town hall. “Billionaires who own these platforms get rich. We all get angry and nobody’s life gets any better. Conspiracy theories don’t put food on the table, put gas in the tank, or improve our communities.”

Paxton, meanwhile, has been battling his own controversies. A series of leaked audio recordings – made during a closed-door meeting – have been posted online and revealed him being critical of his own party and campaign leaders in DC.

Paxton entered the race with a history of scandals. He was impeached by the Texas state legislature in 2023 on allegations including bribery and abuse of public trust, though he was later acquitted. Paxton’s wife of almost four decades, Angela Paxton, then filed for divorce in 2025 on “biblical grounds”, citing adultery.
But Trump endorsed Paxton to run against Talarico, passing up incumbent Republican John Cornyn.

articles.title: White House defends new press secretary amid questions about her legal credentials
articles.summary: Katie Zacharia does not appear to be registered to the legal bar in any state where she has lived.

blocks.text: The White House is defending its new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, as she faces scrutiny over her legal credentials.
President Donald Trump described Zacharia as an attorney when announcing her appointment last week and she has referred to herself as a lawyer.
But when she was asked on Tuesday by a reporter in which state she had passed the bar exam required to be an attorney in the US, she said standing alongside the president: "When I moved to China."

She does not appear to be registered to the bar in any state where she has lived. White House communications director Steven Cheung said Zacharia is "uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people".
Responding to questions about her credentials, Zacharia said in a statement this week: "I practised international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials."
On Wednesday, a watchdog group, Campaign for Accountability, filed a complaint with the California State Bar Association.
They are seeking an investigation into whether Zacharia "repeatedly held herself out to the public as entitled to practise law without a licence to do so, conduct California law treats as a crime".
The 42-year-old political strategist graduated from law school at Pepperdine University in California in 2011, the university confirmed.
A law degree is not a licence to practise law in the US.
The new White House press secretary told the New York Times on Wednesday that when she first began appearing on cable news, she had asked Pepperdine how she should identify herself.
She said she was advised by the university president that she could call herself a lawyer, but not an attorney.

Zacharia took the bar exam in California after graduating from law school but did not pass, according to the Wall Street Journal. California's bar exam is widely regarded as one of the hardest in the US to pass.
A person with direct knowledge of the matter told the outlet that Zacharia took the exam around the same time that she was planning a wedding and preparing to move to China with her husband-to-be.
She moved to Beijing because of her husband's job at an American private equity firm. Zacharia has said she worked on "international transaction law" there.
Her LinkedIn profile states that she worked as an associate at Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from 2011-13.
In China, only Chinese citizens are eligible to obtain a licence to practise law. Foreign employees may work at law firms in other roles.

In February last year, Zacharia said on conservative radio programme The Clay Travis and Buck Sexton Show that she had worked as outside counsel for the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the World Bank during her time in China.
The BBC has contacted the World Bank and IFC for comment.
It is understood the World Bank Group sometimes retains outside law firms, and that those firms decide which of their lawyers are assigned to which parts of any work.
Zacharia has also served as general counsel for Fix California, a conservative non-profit started by Trump ally Ric Grenell, according to her LinkedIn profile.

articles.title: Brazil cuts work week to 40 hours in win for Lula ahead of runoff
articles.summary:
Congress approves constitutional amendment that bans six-day workweeks, which could effect up to 30 million

Brazil’s congress has approved a constitutional amendment to shorten the working…
articles.byline: Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: Brazil’s congress has approved a constitutional amendment to shorten the working week to a maximum of 40 hours, a move that could affect 30 million workers and that will hand a political victory to the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ahead of the presidential runoff in under two weeks.

In an attempt to overturn the first-round lead secured by his opponent, far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, Lula has strongly championed the amendment, which will give some workers an extra day off each week.

Bolsonaro, by contrast, spent months opposing the change but reversed course on Tuesday, saying “the majority of Brazilian workers” supported it. On Wednesday, he joined 75 senators who approved the reform, which passed the lower house in May.
Only one senator voted against it: Hamilton Mourão, former vice-president to Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio’s father.
The constitutional amendment bans six-day workweeks, currently worked by 16 million people, while cutting the maximum workweek from 44 to 40 hours for more than 30 million workers.

The change is expected to affect mainly workers in retail, restaurants and hotels, most of them low-paid – one of the groups which Lula lost the most support from since the 2022 election, when he defeated Jair Bolsonaro.

blocks.caption: Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Photograph: Evaristo Sa/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Lula celebrated the amendment’s passing, writing on social media “ending the 6x1 schedule is about more than changing working hours. It means more time to live, rest, be with family, watch your children grow up, look after yourself and enjoy life.”
Victor Escobar, a researcher at the Laboratory of Parties, Elections and Comparative Politics, said the change “could indeed benefit Lula’s re-election campaign”.
The proposal began as a TikTok movement called Life Beyond Work, founded by a pharmacy assistant who entered politics after its success and later was embraced by Lula.

His party spent months pushing the senate to put the proposal to a vote and many believed that after the far right’s sweeping victory last week secured a broad congressional majority in 2027, the Senate would no longer vote on it.
But Senate president Davi Alcolumbre, whose relationship with Lula has at times been rocky, put it to a vote.
Flávio Bolsonaro’s party had considered blocking it, but polls showed the change had more than 70% of the general population behind it, and more than half of the senator’s voters.
In May, Bolsonaro said the proposal could cause “mass unemployment”, an argument employers’ associations opposed to the change have repeatedly made.
The senator voted remotely while campaigning in the country’s south.

Even after changing his position, Bolsonaro said on Tuesday that he “supports something even better,” referring to an alternative proposal he had long advocated in which pay would be based on the hours actually worked. The Folha newspaper reported that he told business leaders that, if elected, he would review parts of the new amendment, a point several allied senators also made during Wednesday’s vote.

blocks.caption: Brazil’s right-wing Senator and presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro delivers a speech on Wednesday.  Photograph: Sílvio Ávila/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Despite its approval, none of the changes will take effect before the runoff on 25 October. After the Senate president promulgates it, a 60-day period will follow before six-day workweeks are abolished and the maximum working week is reduced from 44 to 42 hours, then to 40 hours after a further 14 months.

However, Escobar believes its approval could already benefit Lula: “It will speak to how voters feel economically when they cast their ballot; they can feel more relieved with a change in their working schedule”.

Marilane Oliveira Teixeira, a professor and researcher at a study centre at the University of Campinas who has spent months examining the possible impacts of the change, said there was no shortage of evidence showing how harmful having only one day off is to workers.

“People who work a 6x1 schedule are practically prevented from having even a minimum level of social life,” she said, adding that the negative effects could include illness, workplace risks and exhaustion, “especially for women, who still carry the burden of unpaid domestic work”.

Lilian Cristo dos Santos, 50, has only one day off from her job as a saleswoman at a home appliances shop in Salvador, Bahia. “There’s no time to go to the doctor, to the beach, to the salon, to look after myself; I wanted to have time to study and I can’t. On my only day off, I have to clean the house and look after my family,” she said.
Santos said she voted for Lula, but has colleagues who chose Bolsonaro. “They say he represents change – well, yes, but certainly for the worse.”

Escobar is among many political scientists who believe that, despite Bolsonaro’s lead, Lula has gained momentum not only from the change to the working schedule, but also from demonstrations by his supporters that have drawn thousands across the country and an effort to build a stronger presence on social media.

Lula also continued announcing benefits just days before the vote, including debt relief for microentrepreneurs, and published a letter to evangelical Christians – who have historically favoured Bolsonaro – stressing his commitment “to ensuring that everyone has two days off a week, because life is not just about work”.

Escobar said: “Although most people have already decided their vote, there are some who are more responsive to political moves, and Lula has been trying very strongly to reach them. … The race still looks somewhat tangled, tied, with some degree of advantage for Bolsonaro, but it is still a very open election.”

articles.title: Retired US generals call on Pentagon to cancel 'barbaric' execution livestream
articles.summary: Livestreaming the execution of Nidal Hasan "will taint the honor of the military that employs it, and a nation that allows it," 72 former officers said in a letter.

blocks.text: A group of 72 retired US generals, admirals, and other high-ranking military officers are pressing the US government to cancel plans to livestream an execution by firing squad.

"We ask the President, our Congressional representatives, and our fellow citizens to act to prevent this barbaric abuse of authority," they wrote in a letter where they also argued the livestream would turn the mass killer into a "martyr".
Last week, the Pentagon announced it would publicly show the 3 December execution of Nidal Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who shot dead 13 unarmed US soldiers at the Fort Hood military base.
Lawmakers from both parties, as well as religious leaders, have criticised the plan.

Last week President Donald Trump said he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan, but some administration officials are now leaning against it, according to CBS News, the BBC's US media partner. CBS reported thatTrump had not yet made a final decision on the livestream as of Tuesday.

In the open letter released on Wednesday, the former military leaders - which included 45 generals, 12 admirals and several former judge advocates general - said they did not oppose the death penalty being carried out.

But they argued a public execution would violate the US Constitution's protections against cruel and unusual punishment and turn what should be a "solemn and grave punishment" into "a carnival for the enjoyment of voyeurs and spectators".
"This type of exploitative broadcasting - that debases human dignity- will taint the honor of the military that employs it, and a nation that allows it," they also wrote.

"It will be used by our nation's enemies to stoke hatred, harm American soldiers and citizens in the future, and will ensure that Hasan becomes a martyr for attacking and killing his fellow soldiers."
The letter's signatories came from throughout the military and included a handful of officers who retired during Trump's first term. Some also had served during the Iraq and Afghanistan wars.

Hasan said in court that he carried out the shooting at Fort Hood, the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American base, believing he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military. Hasan was shot during the attack and now uses a wheelchair.

Retired Maj Gen Tony Taguba, who led the Army's investigation into reported prisoner abuses at Abu Ghraib in Iraq, and retired Air Force Coll Moe Davis, a prosecutor at the Guatanamo Bay detention centre who called waterboarding torture, signed the letter.
So did Charles Bolden, a US Marine Corps Major General who became the head of Nasa, and a retired Lt Gen Claudia Kennedy, the first woman to become a three-star general in the Army.

articles.title: No talks about VP Sara replacement amid impeachment trial --Palace
articles.summary: Thoughts of a possible replacement for Vice President Sara Duterte amid the ongoing impeachment trial is far from President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr's mind, according to Palace Press Officer…

blocks.text: Published October 15, 2026 10:16am

Thoughts of a possible replacement for Vice President Sara Duterte amid the ongoing impeachment trial is far from President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr's mind, according to Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro.
"Hindi po naiisip ng Pangulo yan, sa totoo. Hindi po napaguusapan. Sa ngayon, kahit kami ay nag-memeeeting, hindi napaguusapan ang impeachment," Castro said in an interview on Unang Balita on Friday.
(The President doesn't actually think about that, to be honest. It’s not being discussed. Even when we hold meetings, impeachment is not brought up.)
"Ang nais lang po talaga niya ay due process," Castro added.
(All he really wants is due process.)
Previously, Malacañang also said that nobody will interfere with Duterte's decision to remain on her post amid her impeachment trial.
Duterte on Tuesday said she "will not resign, will never resign from the Office of the Vice President" amid her impeachment trial and the allegations against her.
"Kung hindi po siya magre-resign, desisyon niya po 'yan. Walang manghihimasok diyan. Pero ang pagsasabi niya na mag-resign ang Pangulo, 'yan ay malaking kalokohan," she added.
(If she chooses not to resign, that is her decision. No one will interfere with that. But for her to say that the President should resign, that is utter nonsense.)
Articles of impeachment

On Tuesday the House prosecution panel dropped three out of the four Articles of Impeachment leveled against Duterte, saying its case will stand on Article II alone on alleged unexplained wealth due to non-full declaration of assets and non-divestment of business.
Duterte's camp said the prosecution's withdrawal of three articles of impeachment os an admission that the allegations hurled against her lacked basis.
Duterte's camp has criticized the move of the prosecutors.
Castro, however, asked why the defense team did not object to the dropping of the articles.
"Ang pagbitiw sa articles of impeachment, hindi naman natin nakitaan ng objection yung defense team, nagbigay lang sila ng manifestation. But the team did not give any objection," said Castro.
(Regarding the withdrawal of the articles of impeachment, we did not see any objection from the defense team; they merely had a manifestation. But the team did not raise any objection.)

"So, parang wala naman dapat sisihin dito, kasi parang sinisisi nila ang prosecution, yung senador judges, poero kung babasahin mo lahat, mapapanood mo lahat ng hearing, wala tayong marririnig na objection, iba yung objection sa manifestation," she added.

(So, it seems there’s no one to blame here—though it appears they are blaming the prosecution and the senator-judges—but if you read everything and watch all the hearings, you won’t hear any objections; an objection is different from a manifestation.) —VAL, GMA News

· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Oct 14, 2026 9:21 PM EDT | Last Updated: 6 minutes ago
The B.C. Lumber Trade Council says Canadian softwood lumber now faces total import taxes of almost 35 per cent after the latest review from the U.S. Department of Commerce.
The organization representing B.C. lumber producers says the new figure is down from the combined rate of 45 per cent announced in August last year.
But Kim Haakstad, the council's interim president, says its members are disappointed that Canadian lumber producers still face unjustified and punitive trade measures.
She says in a statement that the combined weight of duties and tariffs remains a significant burden on producers.
The statement says the softwood lumber dispute has dragged on for nearly a decade, putting pressure on forest-dependent communities.

The alleged co-conspirator in a February school shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., was indicted by a grand jury on Wednesday. (Lois Silver/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: British Columbia·New

A grand jury in Washington state has indicted an alleged co-conspirator in the Tumbler Ridge, B.C., mass shooting. The indictment of 30-year-old James Bryant for conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country means there is probable cause for prosecutors to pursue the case.
U.S. Department of Justice says the indictment details acts taken to further February school shooting
A grand jury in Washington state has indicted an alleged co-conspirator in the Tumbler Ridge, B.C., mass shooting.
The indictment of 30-year-old James Bryant for conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country means there is probable cause for prosecutors to pursue the case.
Emily Langlie, a spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney's Office, said last week that an indictment would mean a preliminary hearing in the case scheduled for Oct. 20 would be eliminated.
Bryant, whose lawyers say uses she/her pronouns and goes by the name Melody, was denied bail a day ahead of Wednesday's indictment.
U.S. resident allegedly gave advice, money to Tumbler Ridge shooter
A statement issued by the U.S. Department of Justice says the indictment "details several overt acts that Bryant took to further the school shooting conspiracy."
Eight victims were shot dead in Tumbler Ridge by 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar in February, including five students and a teacher at a secondary school.

The indictment of Bellingham, Wash., resident Bryant lists that she allegedly agreed to record the shooting and broadcast it over the internet, offered the shooter advice on where to attack and what weapons to use and sent Van Rootselaar money to buy a lighter for use in an improvised explosive device.

blocks.text: The Justice Department's statement says conspiracy to murder in a foreign country is punishable by up to life in prison.

It cautions that the accusations against Bryant remain unproven, and says the case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Todd Greenberg with help from the Justice Department’s National Security Division.
Van Rootselaar shot herself dead at the school on Feb. 10.

blocks.text: World·New
The new White House press secretary is facing mounting questions about her background and resume as she transitions into her role as the public face of the Trump administration.
No evidence so far that self-described lawyer has passed any state's bar exam

Katie Zacharia has long described herself as a lawyer as she has worked to establish herself as a commentator for conservative outlets like Fox News and Newsmax. But so far, she and the White House have offered no evidence that she passed the bar exam in any state or in China, where she worked for a large law firm years ago.

The questions add to the confusion surrounding U.S. President Donald Trump's decision to hire Zacharia, who had worked for his social media company for only a few months when he announced her appointment and whose debut at the podium on Tuesday has been widely panned.

Afterward, the president was asked by reporters where Zacharia had passed the bar exam, following a report by the independent outlet Popular Information that she did not appear to be licensed in any state.
Trump stepped aside to allow Zacharia to answer.
"When I moved to China," she responded over the sound of Marine One whirring in the background. It is not clear what she had intended to say or whether she had finished the sentence.
New White House press secretary stumbles in first briefing | Hanomansing Live
China's notoriously difficult National Unified Legal Professional Qualification Examination can only be taken by Chinese citizens.

Asked what credentials she held, the White House passed along a statement from Zacharia, who received a bachelor of arts degree from Pepperdine University in 2007 and received her law degree from Pepperdine Caruso School of Law in 2011, according to the school and her LinkedIn bio.
"I practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials," it read.

Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, added that Zacharia was "uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his Administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as press secretary."

According to her LinkedIn profile, Zacharia has been the senior communications adviser at the Trump Media & Technology Group since June and spent two months as deputy assistant secretary for public affairs at the U.S. Department of Homeland Security earlier this year.
U.S. President Donald Trump is seen speaking with reporters on the South Lawn of the White House on Tuesday, with Zacharia looking on from nearby. (Manuel Balce Ceneta/The Associated Press)

From 2011 to 2013, it says, she served as an associate on the international practice team at the Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing. She also worked as the manager of fundraising and communications for Compassion for Migrant Children, which assists the children of migrant workers, from 2012 to 2013.
More recently, it says she served as general counsel for Fix California, a group started by Trump administration official Richard Grenell.
Neither the firm nor the two groups responded to questions about her tenure and background.
On Instagram, Zacharia describes herself as the White House press secretary, "Wife, Mom, & Lawyer" (with four heart emojis after "Mom").

And her official author page at the California Globe, where she wrote occasional commentary, says that, in addition to being a "regular commentator on Fox News, Newsmax," she has "extensive experience in political advocacy, international corporate law, and non-profit work, including time as outside counsel for the World Bank and IFC in Beijing."

items: Zacharia fails to impress in brief debut as White House press secretary
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt to leave job at month's end, Trump says

blocks.text: A June 2026 press release from NovaRed Mining Inc. announcing her appointment to the company's advisory board, which was first reported by Popular Information, said her "professional experience includes work related to international legal and financial transactions, including matters involving organizations associated with the World Bank Group and the International Finance Corporation during her tenure with Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing."

In announcing her hire on his social media site, Trump described Zacharia as "a distinguished Graduate of Pepperdine University, and the Pepperdine Caruso School of Law, an attorney, and a frequent Commentator on outlets, including Fox News and Newsmax."
"She has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning. She is, likewise, a devoted fan and member of MAGA!" he added.
Not listed with state bar
Zacharia is not listed as a member of the state bar in California, where she currently resides, according to a public database.

Rick Coca, a spokesperson for the State Bar of California, the regulatory agency that oversees state licensing, said in a statement that it has "no record of Kate Sharon Zacharia or Kate Sharon Black" or any version of her married or maiden names "having been licensed to practice law in California."
Popular Information said the same was the case in all 50 states it had queried, plus Washington, D.C.

In response, the watchdog group Campaign for Accountability (CfA) filed a complaint Wednesday with the State Bar of California asking it to investigate whether Zacharia misrepresented herself as a lawyer in violation of California law.

"In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn't puffery; it's a crime. The State Bar should investigate whether Ms. Zacharia has misled the public about her credentials and hold her accountable if she has," said CfA executive director Michelle Kuppersmith in a statement.
The State Bar said it could not confirm whether it had received the complaint or were conducting an investigation, citing confidentiality laws.

articles.title: Ombudsman grants over 1,600 SALN requests in a year
articles.summary: In a statement on Wednesday, October 14, the Office of the Ombudsman said that it has granted 1655 SALN requests.

blocks.text: October 15, 2026 | 7:44am
Office of the Ombudsman along Agham Road in Quezon City.
Wikipedia / patrickroque01

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman has granted more than 1,600 requests for Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) a year after the anti-graft office lifted the restrictions on access to these documents by the media and the public.
In a statement on Wednesday, October 14, the Office of the Ombudsman said that it had granted 1,655 SALN requests.
“One of my first acts as Ombudsman was to tear down the barriers to the Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth of public officials,” Remulla said in a statement.
“For years, the public was told to ask the official's permission before seeing what that official owned. We ended that,” he added.
Remulla also stressed that making government officials' financial disclosures accessible to the public is vital to maintaining transparency and accountability.
“Ang yaman ng isang lingkod-bayan ay hindi pribadong usapin. Kapag pera ng bayan ang pinag-uusapan, may karapatan ang bayan na malaman,” he said.
(The wealth of a public servant is not a private matter. When it comes to the people's money, the people have a right to know.)
On Oct. 14, 2025, then newly appointed Ombudsman Remulla lifted the restriction on SALN access imposed by former Ombudsman Samuel Martires.
The previous requirement for access to an official’s SALN barred the public and the media from obtaining copies of officials’ disclosures without a notarized letter of authority from the declarant.

articles.title: North Korea says it tested cruise missiles to be launched from sub
articles.summary: North Korean state media said the military test-fired cruise missiles designed to be launched from submarines. Pyongyang has ramped up weapons launches in recent weeks.

image.caption: North Korea has carried out similar tests before too [Photo: North Korean photo of what it said was a submarine-launched cruise missile test, 2024]Image: KCNA via REUTERS

blocks.text: North Korea said Wednesday it test-fired cruise missiles designed to be fired from submarines to test the readiness of the country's underwater combat systems and strengthen the Navy's capabilities.
North Korea's state media said it carried out the tests in waters off the east coast of the Korean peninsula.
A North Korean state media report described the weapons as strategic, implying an intent to arm them with nuclear warheads.
But the report did not specify whether they were launched from an actual submarine or an underwater test platform.
North Korea has pushed ahead with modern missile submarines and both ballistic and cruise missile developments.

blocks.caption: People in South Korea watching the news about North Korea having fired ballistic missiles toward the East Sea on October 12Image: Kim Hong-Ji/REUTERS

blocks.text: Pyongyang has tested various weapons in recent weeks to sharpen its military deterrence against the United States and South Korea, but it is not ​yet believed to ‌have launched a modern missile submarine in full operation.
What lessons is North Korea learning from the Iran war?
What to know about North Korea's relations with South Korea and the US

The latest development comes two days after the North Korean state media released photos of the North Korean leader, Kim Jong Un, visiting a new military museum in an undisclosed location in the country.
The museum displayed an intercontinental ballistic missile reportedly capable of reaching the US, photos released by KNCA state media showed.
Kim has made clear that boosting his country's nuclear arsenal was his key priority. Denuclearization, as the US has pushed for, is off the table in this case.
Relations between the North Korean leader and US President Donald Trump also appear to have quieted since the two haven't met in recent years.
US President Donald Trump, during his first term, met Kim three times. Earlier in the week, Trump, alluding to a trip to Asia next month, said he might meet Kim on the trip.
North Korea has put a halt to all coordination with South Korea and has removed all references to reunification with the South from its constitution.

articles.title: Sexual assault reported at frat house near University of Chicago
articles.summary:
Alleged assault follows report of gang rape at frat house at Cornell, which ignited national uproar and criticism online

A 21-year-old woman reported being sexually assaulted last weekend at…

blocks.text: A 21-year-old woman reported being sexually assaulted last weekend at a fraternity house near the University of Chicago, as Greek life nationwide faces renewed scrutiny for recurrent misconduct.
The incident allegedly took place on Sunday at about 1.50am at the off-campus Alpha Epsilon Pi residence, according to a university daily crime log.
In a police report obtained by the Chicago Sun-Times, the woman said she was “not fully conscious” when she was found partially undressed inside a bathroom with a man, who was also semi-nude.
She told police, according to the report, that a group had blocked her friends, at first, from entering the bathroom.
A person of interest has been identified, according to university officials.
The individual is not a student and has been banned from campus, they announced on Wednesday.
No one is in custody, Chicago police said on Wednesday afternoon, adding that an investigation remains ongoing.
Jonathan Pierce, a spokesperson for the fraternity, said on Wednesday there was no evidence its members had participated in the assault or were aware of it.

“When AEPi members (there were several “sober monitors” during the party, including the chapter’s safety officer) became aware of the victim’s report, they offered assistance by providing food and water and even loaned a shirt to the victim as she reported being cold while she waited outside for emergency response,” Pierce said.
“We are pleased that the alleged assailant has been identified and hope that the victim can find some solace in knowing that justice is being done.”

The alleged assault follows a harrowing report of a gang-rape at a Cornell University fraternity house in 2024. Recent news of the purported attack ignited national uproar and criticism of the Ivy League school’s perceived leniency toward the alleged offenders.
New York state prosecutors have reopened an investigation into the report.
Under mounting backlash, Cornell has also suspended all fraternity parties for the remainder of the academic year, as it assesses the safety of its Greek societies.

Last week, the University of Arizona took a similar move, halting all fraternity activity in the wake of several hazing and physical assault allegations, including accusations of a Greek organization coercing recruits into binge drinking and swallowing live goldfish.

articles.title: Volodymyr Zelenskyy feels ‘betrayed’ by Donald Trump over Starlink access
articles.summary:
Ukrainian president accused US president of picking the other side after four years of war

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he feels personally betrayed by Donald Trump after it emerged that…
articles.byline: Dan Sabbagh, Jessica Elgot and Andrew Roth in Kyiv

blocks.text: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he feels personally betrayed by Donald Trump after it emerged that Ukraine’s military has had its access to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite squeezed, raising doubts about long-term US support for Kyiv.

The Ukrainian president, on a visit to London, accused Trump of picking the other side after more than four years of war, risking a breakdown in relations already strained by the US agreeing to buy diesel from Moscow.

Ahead of a meeting with prime minister Andy Burnham in Downing Street, Zelenskyy appeared in a TV interview where he was asked whether the sudden restriction of Starlink was deliberate and if he felt betrayed by Trump.

“Really, yes … but it’s a little bit more complicated ⁠than just my emotions or my feelings,” the Ukrainian president replied, adding: “It’s a pity that we are losing, we are losing a strong partner.”

Overnight, Ukraine’s military reported that, without explanation, the Starlink satellite communications system, produced by Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, was no longer working at speeds greater than 100mph.

That effectively rendered most of the drones used by Ukraine to strike behind the frontlines inoperable – and, it later emerged, affected the most effective air defence system to stop Russian jet-powered attack drones bombing Kyiv.

“I am sure they knew what they did, absolutely. Because it was 1am at night, Starlink was blocked by SpaceX and the United States,” Zelenskyy said in an interview with Piers Morgan. “This decision will bring a lot of human losses … of course, people will die.”

The sudden outage came as Russia launched ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US for a second night. For years, the US has provided Ukraine with intelligence when strikes were about to take place.

Trump denied that his administration had cut intelligence sharing on Tuesday, but Zelenskyy said in an interview with US broadcaster NPR, aired on Wednesday, that military advisers had received threats from the US that intelligence sharing could be limited in the future.

The US president has demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil refineries, which he has blamed for the high cost of diesel, although most analysts say the closure of the strait of Hormuz after the US-Israel attack on Iran has had a far larger impact on global energy prices.

blocks.caption: Andy Burnham greeted Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, warmly at No 10. Photograph: Henry Nicholls/Reuters

blocks.text: The two leaders fell out in the spring of 2025 during a disastrous visit by Zelenskyy to the Oval Office, where the US president said: “You don’t have the cards” to win the war. The row was followed by a brief pause in intelligence sharing and a desperate scramble by European allies to calm the row.

Burnham met Zelenskyy in Downing Street on Wednesday, hours after he promised MPs that the Ukrainian president “would not leave empty-handed” and that he had tasked officials with drawing up further sanctions and options for speeding up military aid.

As the pair met at No 10, he promised that Britain’s support for Ukraine would remain constant. “You have seen the solidarity and the support you have got from everybody here in Britain. We are behind you and that will not change,” he said.
Zelenskyy had met King Charles in Buckingham Palace earlier on Wednesday.
In brief remarks to reporters, Zelenskyy said he hoped to raise access to Starlink and intelligence sharing in his meeting with the British prime minister.

Burnham pledged that he would accelerate the supply of British lightweight multi-role missiles to Ukraine, which the country uses to counter Russian drone strikes and said they were looking for “all possible avenues” of further support.
The prime minister also said he was prepared to discuss the ceasefire proposed by Trump on attacks on energy infrastructure but acknowledged that Moscow had not abided by it.
“Sadly, what we have seen from Russia is further attacks on critical national infrastructure in Ukraine,” he said.

Earlier Burnham told MPs at PMQs that he wanted to be “careful” about potential criticism of Trump that might risk exacerbating tensions, saying he was “laying the ground” for a reconciliation: “I will listen to President Zelenskyy carefully, but he won’t be going away from Britain today empty-handed.”
The UK is also set to give £17m in funding towards repairs to the protective roof over the destroyed Chornobyl nuclear power plant which was damaged by Russian drone strike last year.

The meeting, which lasted just over an hour, began as Burnham greeted Zelenskyy with a hug on Downing Street, before the pair walked to the door of No 10 and posed for photographs, flanked by Irish Guards in full ceremonial uniform.

Musk said the decision to curtail Starlink was not one made by him. The communications system is not directly licensed to clients who are using weapons, and the Ukrainian military was linked to a related network called Starshield, which is operated by the US government.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk said, referring to Trump.

Terminals travelling at more than 100mph and using a version of Starlink for the military and other national security agencies suddenly lost connectivity, said Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser on military technology to Zelenskyy, in what appeared to be a targeted outage meant to disrupt military operations.

“Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” said Beskrestnov, who is also a popular military blogger. “It’s clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation.”

Limiting Starlink’s access speeds would have a significant effect on Ukraine’s air defences because it is being used, according to Beskrestnov, in “the most current effective solution”: interceptors that target the jet-powered Shahed drones now deployed in large numbers to bomb Ukraine.

“With their actions, our partners are depriving us of one of the few chances we have to defend ourselves,” he added in a follow-up post. Shahed interception rates had already dropped from more than 90% to about 60% when Russia upgraded its engines to jet power in the early summer.

It also complicates Ukraine’s use of medium-range, mid-strike drones for hitting targets in its territories occupied by Russia. But, ironically, it would have no impact on Ukraine’s deep strike bombing of oil refineries because Kyiv is banned from using Starlink to hit targets inside of Russia.

Russia carried out a massive strike against Ukrainian energy infrastructure late on Tuesday evening, Zelenskyy said, launching 39 ballistic missiles and 120 attack drones against Kyiv and Kharkiv. The strikes hit five big power plants, key substations and other infrastructure that sustains major cities including Kyiv.
At least 600,000 people were now without power, he said, adding that outages could become more widespread.

Trump last week announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine that has not been confirmed. Zelenskyy said he had not heard of the deal until Trump announced it on his Truth Social site, and the Kremlin on Wednesday claimed it was abiding by the ceasefire because Trump had not specified which energy infrastructure it included.
Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin’s spokesperson, told reporters: “The energy truce proposed by Trump was not specified in detail, so it cannot be claimed that Russia is failing to observe it.”

articles.title: Brooklyn novelty shop reeling from 'surreal' row with Kelly Clarkson over mechanical bird
articles.summary: Art of Play says its staff have been threatened after the singer complained online about how she was treated.

blocks.text: On a rainy Wednesday afternoon, a novelty toy and games store in a quiet part of New York City was seeing much busier foot traffic than usual.
Inside, the shop was packed with cameramen and customers, while passersby in this Brooklyn neighbourhood of Cobble Hill looked inside, asking: "Where's the bird?"

Art of Play has found itself at the centre of a social media storm since the weekend when Grammy-winning musician Kelly Clarkson complained online that the boutique store would not let her buy a singing and dancing mechanical bird that was perched on the wall.
The Since U Been Gone singer claimed she was "looked at as if I couldn't afford" the bird - which she said had a price tag of $15,000 (£11,000).

"Y'all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts' character in Pretty Woman," she said, referring to a scene from the 1990 romantic comedy film where Roberts' character is treated poorly by staff at a shop, who imply she cannot afford various items.
In a follow-up post on social media, Clarkson said the store had told her the bird cost $15,000 and that they could find her something else "comparable".
Art of Play has defended how it treated the star on social media, saying the wooden bird - which is called Molly - is permanently attached to the wall and is not for sale.
It said that during Clarkson's five-minute visit on Saturday, an employee suggested to her that she could buy an identical bird for $15,000.
They also said they had offered her a different singing bird for $2,000 from a clock-making shop in Germany, which she could have purchased that day.
"Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by eight million people who have never visited our store," Art of Play said.
"It's been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity."
The kerfuffle lingered in headlines on Wednesday as a news outlet released surveillance video from Art of Play purporting to show Clarkson's visit.
The grainy footage, which has no audio, is said to show her wearing a yellow shirt, a baseball cap and a backpack while browsing items, including Molly the bird.
She can be seen talking with an employee - apparently about the bird as she points at it - and later moving to leave the store. She comes back in to say something animatedly to the cashier.
But while the argument over the bird has gone viral online, some of Art of Play's customers had not heard about it before being greeted by news cameras on the premises.
One customer who was in town visiting his daughter said he was not familiar with the controversy.
For others, Clarkson's claims that those at the store had treated her rudely came as a surprise.
Kiran Ramineni, who lives next door, described Art of Play as a "very nice small mom and pop store" and said he had seen flocks of journalists there in recent days.
Shopgoer Emily Trantanella, 27, said: "I feel like a pretty woman and I've always been treated very well here.
"I really like it here."

articles.title: U.S. 'monitoring' Canada for signs of midterm election interference, ambassador says
articles.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra says American officials are "closely watching" Canadian politicians for signs of election interference ahead of the pivotal midterms next month.

image.caption: U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra said in a recent podcast appearance that American officials are 'closely watching' for election interference by Canadians. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics
U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra says American officials are "closely watching" Canadian politicians for signs of election interference ahead of the pivotal midterms next month.
Hoekstra said U.S. will respond if any actions by Canadians amount to meddling
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Oct 14, 2026 5:15 PM EDT | Last Updated: 6 hours ago
During an interview on The Really Big Show podcast posted last week, Hoekstra said political ads run by the province of Ontario last year could be interpreted as political interference.

U.S. President Donald Trump ended trade talks with Canada in October 2025 after Ontario aired an ad during the World Series using clips of former U.S. president Ronald Reagan criticizing tariffs and supporting free trade.

But Trump has not held back from weighing in on Canadian affairs and the actions of the government on this side of the border: He's repeatedly criticized Canada and made threatening remarks about its sovereignty. As recently as Wednesday, he reiterated his stance that America's northern neighbour should become the 51st U.S. state.
"They'll end up being the 51st state because that's the only way it works," Trump said at a rally in Bullhead City, Arizona.
At the same rally, Trump also grumbled about Canadian tariffs on milk and made mention of his move to rename Lake Ontario on the U.S. side of the border.
Hoekstra calls out Joly, Trudeau
Hoekstra also cited recent comments by Industry Minister Mélanie Joly and former prime minister Justin Trudeau and suggested they also could amount to interference.
Hoekstra warned Canadian politicians to keep their "nose out" of American politics in the weeks before the midterm elections.
Trudeau criticized the Trump administration during a discussion at Brown University on Sept. 22.

"There is a pattern here of doing things that are driving up prices for your consumers and not necessarily making anything better for America, by fighting with one of your oldest and best allies," Trudeau said during the conversation.

items: Alberta referendum could be target for foreign interference, CSIS says
Poilievre shrugs off Elon Musk's pro-separatist posts
Can the U.S.-Canada trade war change course if Democrats win?

blocks.text: In the interview, Hoekstra said Joly made comments about targeting retaliatory tariffs at "politically sensitive states."
Joly pushed back on Wednesday, telling reporters that Canada would never engage in election interference and would "never accept that also being done to us in Canada."
Joly said she has been to the U.S. in recent months and has met with Democrats and Republicans.
Canada 'absolutely not' interfering in U.S. midterms, Joly says

"Fundamentally, what I've done in the U.S. is to attract investments," she said. "I think I'll be able to have good news of investments by different American companies to Canada. And that's exactly what I'm doing and that will continue to be my strategy in the U.S. and also around the world."
Hoekstra said if any actions by Canadians end up amounting to election interference, the United States will respond.
"We're monitoring it, we're evaluating it and if some of it becomes election interference then America will respond to it," Hoekstra said.
The president has been actively campaigning in battleground states ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

The entire House of Representatives and one-third of U.S. Senate seats will be contested. Currently the Republicans hold a majority of seats in both, but polls suggest there is a chance that the Democrats wrest control of both chambers.

The Globe and Mail reported recently that Republican political operatives were on the ground in Alberta earlier this year to help the separatist campaign. CBC News previously reported that Alberta separatists also attended meetings in U.S. State Department offices in Washington, D.C., last year.
In August, Prime Minister Mark Carney ordered the Canadian negotiating team to call off renewed trade talks with the U.S. after accusing the Americans of making unreasonable demands.
Canada-U.S. trade war emerges as key issue ahead of U.S. midterms
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre was in Detroit on Tuesday to make a case for tariff-free trade in the auto sector.
"We have a 200-year-old relationship. There's always going to be grievances on both sides of the border," he said on CNN.
"We have our grievances with the United States even predating this most recent trade dispute, but I would focus on what we can do together."

items: Federal intelligence agency contacted as U.S. interference claims swirl in Quebec election

blocks.text: Hoekstra's comments come after one Trump's trade advisers threatened repercussions for Canada if it "interferes" in the upcoming midterms.
Peter Navarro dismissed Canada's approach to trade talks during an economic conference in Washington last month, saying that Canadian lobbyists need to "get the hell out of our country."
"The problem you have is you lobby this country and you've been successful in the past and you think you can keep doing that," Navarro said of Canada's approach.
'You will pay': Trump adviser warns Canada not to 'interfere' with U.S. midterms
"Memo to Canada: You cannot do that. That game is up and if you interfere in our elections in Maine or Michigan you will pay even more dearly."
The trade war has become a pressure point on Republican candidates running for the Senate in the two border states Navarro mentioned.
Just last week, the Republican candidate for Michigan's open Senate seat released a new 30-second ad criticizing tariffs.
"Here in Michigan we know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end this tariff war now," Mike Rogers says in the ad.
Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who has represented Maine since 1997, has also tried to distance herself from Trump's tariffs.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Catherine Morrison is a reporter for The Canadian Press.
With files from CBC News

articles.title: Musk says any limits on Ukraine's Starlink access down to US, not his firm
articles.summary: Ukraine says Starlink access has improved but it is still facing speed limits which are disrupting its battlefield "missions".

blocks.text: Elon Musk has suggested that the US government may be behind restrictions on the speed at which some of Ukraine's weapons can travel and stay connected to SpaceX's Starlink internet network.

Starlink is a vital tool allowing Kyiv to guide drones to Russian targets and also protect its own skies, but on Tuesday night Ukraine said unexpected new speed limits were disrupting its battlefield missions.
An adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky said he believed the restrictions were not a coincidence and were related to the latest strains between Kyiv and Washington.

Musk said that Starshield, the military-grade sister service to Starlink, is controlled by the US government, and "any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately [the US president]".

Musk - writing on X - had been responding to pleas from Ukrainian officials to restore connectivity, including from Zelensky who told UK media: "I hope that it's a mistake, maybe (a) huge technical problem. I don't know, but we are asking to... switch (it) on."
Starlink, which is owned by Musk's SpaceX, restricted speed limits on Tuesday night to 100mph (160km/h), meaning any weapons that travelled faster than that lost connectivity to the network.
It had been partially restored by Wednesday evening, Ukraine's former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov said.
"Removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense," he wrote on X, thanking Elon Musk and asking for his "continued support".
About an hour later, Musk replied to that post, defending his company's involvement.
"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he wrote.
Musk added that Starlink is for "civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company".
The US government has not commented.

While both companies are owned by Musk's SpaceX, Starlink is a civilian service that uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide internet access, particularly in remote areas, while Starshield is designed for government and military use.

The restrictions on Tuesday night came as Russia launched deadly attacks against Ukraine that killed several people in Kyiv, officials said, and hit communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military.
President Zelensky said it was "one of the largest attacks" from Russia, and while "a significant part of the drones were shot down" there were "also hits".
At least 600,000 people across Ukraine were left without electricity, and residents said they received no warning of incoming drones before they hit.
"It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation, Zelensky's adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram on Wednesday morning.
US President Donald Trump has grown increasingly frustrated towards Ukraine as it continues to strike Russian energy facilities.
Zelensky has said that the US threatened to restrict intelligence sharing if he did not sign up to Trump's energy ceasefire, but on Tuesday, Trump denied this.
Speaking during a visit to London on Wednesday, President Zelensky agreed that he had felt betrayed after the US made a deal with Russia to import 300,000 tonnes of its of diesel.
"Really yes... but it's a little bit more complicated than just my emotions or my feelings," Zelensky said, when asked by UK journalist Piers Morgan if he felt betrayed.
During his one-day visit, Zelensky was greeted with a hug by UK PM Andy Burnham at Downing Street and held an audience with King Charles.
Ahead of the president's arrival, No 10 announced it would speed up delivery of lightweight multirole missiles to Ukraine, which have been used to bring down Russian drones.
"We are behind you and that will not change," Burnham told Zelensky.

articles.title: What to know about the deadly U.K. tiger attack — and the 'offensive' video shared by Trump
articles.summary: The family of a man mauled to death by a tiger at a U.K. wildlife park on Saturday is pleading with people to stop sharing footage of the attack online, calling it "deeply offensive" and painful. The…

image.caption: A sign marks the entrance to Yorkshire Wildlife Park near Doncaster, England. William Chapman, 23, was mauled to death by a tiger on Saturday after entering the animal's enclosure at the park. (Annabel Lee-Ellis/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: The family of a man mauled to death by a tiger at a U.K. wildlife park on Saturday is pleading with people to stop sharing footage of the attack online, calling it "deeply offensive" and painful.

The statement from the family of 23-year-old William Chapman came after U.S. President Donald Trump shared a clip of the fatal attack on his Truth Social platform Tuesday, writing "don't ⁠ever mess with nature!"

The 41-second video shared by Trump shows a large tiger repeatedly biting and clawing at Chapman. Trump's post was then shared by the White House's Rapid Response account on X, where commenters called it "sick" and "disgusting."
The U.S. president later posted ​an apparently AI-generated video depicting himself taming a tiger ​and then playing with it, accompanied by the song The Lion Sleeps Tonight.
His social media posts have sparked outrage, but they have also raised questions about how the tragedy happened.
Here's what we know about the tiger attack and the man who died.
Where did this happen?
The attack happened on Saturday in a tiger enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park near Doncaster in northern England.

The popular conservation and welfare park opened in 2009. The "Land of the Tigers" area opened in 2011, "where the majestic big cats can freely roaming their woodlands and grasslands or play in their very own waterfall pool," the park explains on its website.
It features a 300-metre-long raised walkway for spectators.
Victim's family pleads for respect after Trump shares tiger attack video
How did the attack happen?

BBC News reports that emergency services were called to the park in the early afternoon Saturday for reports that a man had climbed into the tiger enclosure from a high walkway. Witnesses told multiple U.K. media outlets that the tiger had been lounging on a ledge until the man entered.
"The tiger got alerted. He went into stalk mode. The tiger came flying off the ledge and approached him," a witness told The Telegraph.

Witnesses reportedly tried to distract the tiger, shouting at it and banging on the fence, as the animal pawed and nipped at the man. Videos posted online appear to show the man pointing at the tiger, yelling "stop" and "no."

items: Image of mournful elephant mom wins 2026 Wildlife Photographer of the Year
'He was fighting,' says mother of western Manitoba man killed in animal attack

blocks.text: Staff reportedly erected screens to block the view as emergency services responded.

In a Facebook post, South Yorkshire Police confirmed that "despite the best efforts of medical personnel, the man was pronounced dead at the scene." The park was then evacuated, police said, adding there was no risk to the public.
Yorkshire Wildlife Park was closed and has yet to reopen to the public. The park is "working closely with the authorities," it notes on its website.
A coroner's inquest is scheduled to begin Thursday, reports the Doncaster Free Press.
William Chapman in an undated photo posted to Facebook by South Yorkshire Police on Wednesday. (South Yorkshire Police/Facebook)
Who was William Chapman?
Chapman, 23, was a former child actor, according to the BBC. The outlet notes he appeared in the 2009 ITV production May Contain Nuts and the 2012 BBC series True Stories.
The Jackie Palmer Stage School in High Wycombe shared a tribute to Chapman on Facebook Tuesday, noting he was a former student.
"We loved watching William grow, both as a person and as a performer, during his time with us," the school posted.
"It was a privilege to be part of his journey, and he will be remembered with great fondness by everyone who had the pleasure of knowing him."
Chapman's family described him as a "bright, warm and engaging young man whom his family dearly loved" in a statement shared by South Yorkshire Police.
"Sadly, William suffered from significant mental illness over a number of years and was consequently prescribed strong medication," the family added.
The statement said it was for the coroner to determine whether his medical history played a role in his death.
"The family are hopeful that the relevant authorities will do their utmost to get to the bottom of why our amazing son did what he did."
A Facebook tribute to William Chapman posted by the Jackie Palmer Stage School and Agency on Tuesday. (Jackie Palmer Stage School and Agency/Facebook)
How did he get in the enclosure?
Chapman reportedly entered it himself.

A witness told the Daily Mail that Chapman had been "dancing his way up and down the bridge with his AirPods in" before asking her to take a photo of him. Witnesses told the Telegraph that, shortly after, another woman tried to stop Chapman from jumping in but he overpowered her.
Witnesses described Chapman acting "in a trance" in the enclosure, sometimes dancing with his phone out.

Several U.K. media outlets reported that he uploaded a video of himself approaching the tiger in the enclosure to his Instagram account moments before he was attacked. His account has since been made private.

"He had arms wide open ready for the tiger to attack him. It was quite bad. We were just stood there, frozen… the last thing we saw was the tiger’s jaw on his neck," Scarlet Hogan, 21, told the Telegraph.

Observers online have pointed out that in the videos circulating online, Chapman appears to clench both fists with his little fingers pointing out. They suggest this may be the sign for "bad" in Makaton, an alternative form of sign language for people with limited speech.
These reports have not been confirmed.
A photo of William Chapman posted by South Yorkshire Mayor Oliver Coppard on Wednesday. (Oliver Coppard/Facebook)
What happens to the tiger?
The tiger involved in the attacked, named Altai, is "safe and well" and will not be euthanized, the park said in a statement posted on Instagram on Sunday.
The tigers at Yorkshire Wildlife Park are all endangered Amur tigers, also known as Siberian tigers. They're the largest big cats in the world.
An animal ranger at the park quoted by the Telegraph said it wasn't the tiger's fault, and that to the animal, Chapman was "just something else to play with."
"The keepers are all distraught," she added.
The park welcomed Altai in a 2025 Instagram post, saying he had just arrived from a zoo in Norway.
An Instagram post by Yorkshire Wildlife Park from 2025 shows Altai, the Amur tiger that mauled a man in an enclosure on Saturday. (Yorkshire Wildlife Park/Instagram)
Why did Trump post about it?
Trump has not offered an explanation for his posts about Chapman.
The U.S. president regularly uses social media to make commentary and share AI-generated images and videos. In April, for instance, Trump posted an image that appeared to depict himself as Jesus.
Chapman's family, in their statement, asked people to "please stop" sharing footage.
"The family are utterly devastated by their loss and are struggling to come to terms with what has happened," the family said.
"The publication and circulation of deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress at an exceptionally vulnerable time."
South Yorkshire Mayor Oliver Coppard was among those to condemn Trump's posts.

"The President of the United States now using AI to mock that incident and the pain felt by the family … for little more than a cheap laugh on social media, should be greeted with the contempt it deserves," Coppard wrote on Facebook on Wednesday.

As of Wednesday, videos of the attack were still being shared across social media platforms including X, Threads and TikTok. The video shared on X by the White House had been viewed around 2.5 million times.
CBC News has contacted X to ask whether it will be removing videos that show the attack, but has yet to hear back.
Trump tries to explain now-deleted Jesus-like AI post

articles.title: Student protesters attack government buildings in Tirana
articles.summary: Thousands of students in Albania are calling for better university conditions and job prospects, but buildings have been set on fire in the unrest.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
The scene in Tirana, Albania's capital on Wednesday
Thousands of students have taken to the streets in the Albanian capital of Tirana, attacking several government buildings on the second day of violent anti-government protests.
The demonstration began outside the ministry of education on Tuesday, as students called for better university conditions and job prospects.
Wednesday saw part of the education ministry's building set on fire, while the prime minister's office, finance and interior ministry, and several surrounding businesses were also attacked.
Albania's Deputy Prime Minister ​Albana Koçiu has called for "calmness, self-restraint and maturity" and said "Albania does not need to burn to change".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Dozens of protesters wearing gas masks and balaclavas were seen throwing rocks and firecrackers through the education ministry's gates

blocks.text: Dozens of protesters wearing gas masks and balaclavas were seen throwing rocks and firecrackers through the education ministry's gates
Riot police have clashed with the protesters, using tear gas and water cannons to disperse them.
One demonstrator, Enida Bimi, told Reuters news agency that the protest is not just for the students, but "for all the people of Albania".

"The people are very angry at the system. They need to change everything. With this corruption all around, the crime and everything else is happening. And the people now are angry. They need to change the system," Bimi said.
Another protester, Arber Leshi, said people are angry at "the most corrupt government our country has ever seen".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Protester Enida Bimi said people "are very angry at the system"

blocks.text: Protester Enida Bimi said people "are very angry at the system"
Officials have criticised the behaviour of some protesters.

"Setting fire to an institution is not a peaceful protest. It is an act that endanger's peoples lives", said economy minister Delina Ibrahimaj, responding to a video appearing to show protesters throwing rocks at the finance ministry building.
Sixteen people were arrested "in connection with violent acts" during Tuesday's protest, Albania's state-run news agency said.
This student-led protest comes after months of anti-government protests, known as the Flamingo Revolution, which is calling for Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.
The protests were sparked by a luxury tourism project linked to Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner in May, which fuelled anger over alleged corruption and a lack of transparency from Rama's government.
